Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

in preposition

where something is: in a place

also in (the writings of)

classical

Hor. C. 2.16.13–14: splendet in mēnsā tenuī salīnum
Vulg. Jo. 14.2: In domō Patris meī mānsiōnēs multae sunt
Traupman 332

in (+ ablative)

preposition with the ablative

in, on (where something is)

The ablative answers “where?” (ubi?); with the accusative in answers “where to?” and means into or onto (see into). English “in” and “on” are both in with the ablative: in urbe, in town; in mēnsā, on the table.

Other words

  • domī, rūrī; Rōmae, Corinthī (locative) — at home, in the country; in Rome, in Corinth

    locative, without a preposition · classical · Plin. NH 19.51: Rōmae quidem per sē hortus ager pauperis erat; Cic. Att. 13.49.1: quam equidem rūrī esse arbitror

    Names of towns and small islands take no preposition: singular nouns of the first and second declensions stand in the locative (Rōmae, Corinthī), the rest in the ablative (Athēnīs, Carthāgine). So do domī, at home, rūrī, in the country, and humī, on the ground. Domī meae, at my house: see at the house of.

  • hōc locō, tōtā domō (ablative alone) — in (with locus, and with tōtus)

    ablative without a preposition · also used · classical · Ov. Met. 11.608–609: jānua … nūlla domō tōtā est

    With locus (hōc locō, eōdem locō), and often with a noun that has tōtus (tōtā urbe), the preposition is left out.

  • apud (+ acc.) — in (the writings of an author)

    also used · classical · Traupman 332

    Apud Platōnem, in Plato.

Examples

  • In domō Patris meī mānsiōnēs multae sunt.

    In my Father’s house are many rooms.Vulg. Jo. 14.2

  • exāmen apum in arbore praetōriō imminente cōnsēderat

    a swarm of bees had settled in a tree overhanging the general’s tentLiv. 21.46.2

  • dōnāstī, Lupe, rūs sub urbe nōbīs; sed rūs est mihi majus in fenestrā

    you have given me a farm outside town, Lupus; but I have a bigger farm in my windowMart. 11.18.1–2

  • Rōmae quidem per sē hortus ager pauperis erat

    at Rome the garden was in itself the poor man’s fieldPlin. NH 19.51

  • Atticae prīmum salūtem (quam equidem rūrī esse arbitror; multam igitur salūtem)

    first, greetings to Attica (who I think is in the country; so, many greetings)Cic. Att. 13.49.1

  • jānua nē versō strīdōrēs cardine reddat, nūlla domō tōtā est

    so that no door may creak as its hinge turns, there is none in the whole houseOv. Met. 11.608–609

See also into, at, on, inside, house.
